title: The horse-drawn vacuum cleaner
hook: The first powered vacuum cleaner was so big it was pulled through London by horses.
peek: In 1901 Hubert Booth built a motor-driven vacuum cleaner the size of a cart. It was parked in the street, and long hoses snaked through the windows to suck dust from carpets inside.
lede: In 1901 the British engineer Hubert Cecil Booth patented a powered machine that sucked dust out of carpets rather than blowing it about. It was enormous. The engine and pump sat on a horse-drawn cart that parked outside a house, and workers fed long hoses in through the windows. Londoners nicknamed the bright red machine Puffing Billy.

bullets.text: Booth had watched a demonstration of a machine that blew dust off railway carriage seats. He thought suction would work better. The story goes that he tested this by pressing a handkerchief to a plush chair and sucking through it, finding a ring of dust.
Booth set up the British Vacuum Cleaner Company to sell cleaning as a service. Customers did not buy the machine; they booked a visit from the cart and its crew.
The company was hired to clean the carpets at Westminster Abbey before the coronation of Edward VII in 1902. Royal interest helped make the idea fashionable.
Society hostesses reportedly held parties where guests watched the dust travel through glass sections of the hose. Seeing how much dirt left the carpets was part of the show.
